svg.aria-label: Three chemical differences between RNA and DNA and their consequences: the presence or absence of the 2-prime hydroxyl and the instability and catalytic possibility it creates, how the difference between thymine and uracil provides a criterion for repair, and single-stranded RNA folding according to its sequence.
svg.text: A The sugar: 2-prime OH or not
deoxyribose
ribose
2' OH
Two consequences of that OH
1 it can attack the neighbouring phosphate, so RNA breaks
(especially in alkali): RNA is unstable, DNA is not
2 a group that can take part in reactions: RNA can be catalytic
B The base: thymine or uracil
cytosine deaminates spontaneously to URACIL
If DNA used uracil as a normal base, damage-derived uracil
could not be told from the real thing.
DNA uses thymine, so any uracil found in DNA IS damage.
Uracil-DNA glycosylase can then remove it. RNA is not kept long, so it needs no such protection — and saves the cost of a methyl group.
C Strandedness: in RNA the sequence becomes the structure
DNA: double helix, nearly uniform shape, good for holding sequence
RNA: single strand that pairs with itself — hairpins, loops, 3-D folds
tRNA's cloverleaf, the ribosome's catalytic centre, the leader RNA's two alternative structures all come from this.
Sequence is structure, and structure is function.
